flow.parent: Keep the samples anonymous. A family should never be shamed because of a test result.

flow.do: Collect the samples. Put each in its own cup with a code number. Write the codes in a list, and keep the list of who gave which one in a separate place.
flow.say: Write a code on each cup. Keep the list of names apart. Why do we do that?
flow.kid: Label each cup with a number.
flow.parent: Using codes keeps the test fair. It also keeps the results honest and kind.

flow.do: Test each sample in the same way. Put a teaspoon of the powder on still water, wait 2 minutes, and write what you see. Put tea on wet paper. Write 'found something' or 'nothing found by this test'. If a sample shows something, test it again with fresh water before you write it down.
flow.say: What does this test say about each sample? What do we write when it finds nothing?
flow.kid: Run the test on every cup. Write 'found something' or 'nothing found by this test'.

ask.q: If most samples show nothing, did you prove that all the food is pure?
good: No. The test can find only what it is built to find.
Nothing found does not mean nothing is there.

flow.parent: Many samples will show nothing, and that is the honest result. Natural turmeric and tea also tint water a little, so use the same test and the same wait for all.

flow.do: Make the table. Count how many samples found something, how many found nothing, and what you did not test, such as lead. Draw a bar chart with three bars.
flow.say: How many samples showed something? How many showed nothing? What did we not test at all?
flow.kid: Count the results. Draw a bar chart.
flow.parent: Include the bar for 'not tested' even though it has no samples counted. It is the honest part of the chart.

flow.do: Write a short honest report in five sentences. Say what was tested, how many samples, what was found, what was not tested and what you would do next. Then write a practice complaint of three sentences. Say what you bought, where you bought it, the batch number and what you noticed. Do not send it unless a real test shows something and a grown-up agrees.
flow.say: Write what we did, what we found and what we cannot say. Then write a practice complaint in three sentences.
flow.kid: Write your report. Then practise a complaint, but do not send it.
flow.think: How is a report that says 'nothing found by these tests' different from one that says 'all our food is pure'? Who might be misled by the second one?
flow.parent: Real complaints can go through the Food Safety Connect app or the state food safety office. Keep the packet and the bill. Only report when you have a real reason.

challenges.title: Build a milk-flow tester: a plate, a slope and a ruler
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. The slanting-plate test is easy to do and easy to do badly. You design a tester that two different people can use to get the same answer.
challenges.problem: Build a milk-flow tester from things at home. It must tell plain milk from half-and-half watered milk. Two different people must get the same ranking.
constraints: Use only things from home, such as plates, trays, books, a ruler, tape and a spoon.
Test plain milk, milk with an equal amount of added water, and plain water.
Test each at least three times.
Both of you must get the same ranking from fastest to slowest.
The milk is never eaten or drunk afterwards.
materials: a clean steel plate or tray
fresh milk, water and a clean spoon
a phone to film the drops, if you wish

setup.art: A steel tray leaning on a stack of books with a paper tape line across the top and a ruler along the side.
setup.caption: 1. Build a slope with a line at the top and a ruler beside it.

setup.art: Three drops of milk, watered milk and water running down the tray in different lanes.
setup.caption: 2. Put three drops on the line together and measure how far each runs in 10 seconds.

setup.art: A table of ten rows comparing the distances that two testers measured for each liquid.
setup.caption: 3. Compare your results with a second tester.

flow.do: Try the plain method first. Tilt a clean plate on books. Put one drop of milk and one drop of watered milk on it. See which runs farther. Ask a second person to do the same. Write down how far each drop ran, if you can. Look at whether the two of you agree.
flow.say: Did you and the other person get the same ranking? What could make your results different?
flow.kid: Try the plain test. Ask a friend to try too. Do you agree?

ask.q: What could make two people's drops run differently?
good: A different slope, a different size of drop or a greasy plate.
Each person may drop them at a different moment.

flow.parent: A greasy plate makes drops run unevenly. Wash it with soap and dry it before every trial.

flow.do: Try the usual fixes. Fix the slope with books so that it is the same every time. Mark a line at the top of the plate with tape. Use the same spoon tip to make a drop of about the same size. Put all the drops on the line together. Measure how far each ran in 10 seconds with a ruler. Do it three times and write the distances.
flow.say: Which fix made the results more similar from one try to the next?
flow.kid: Fix the slope and the line. Measure how far each drop runs in 10 seconds.
flow.parent: Use a ruler laid beside the plate on the same side each time.

flow.do: Try a surprising fix. Film the drops with a phone placed on books. Play the film at slow speed and count how long each drop takes to reach a line 10 centimetres down. Or tape paper strips down the plate to make lanes, so that each drop runs in its own lane. Write the times or the distances.
flow.say: Is a film more exact than your eyes? Why do lanes help?
flow.kid: Film the drops and watch slowly. Or tape lanes so that drops cannot meet.
flow.parent: A lane stops drops from touching. If two drops touch, they join and run differently.

flow.do: Compare all the methods. For each one, see whether two people got the same ranking, and whether the numbers were close on three tries. Choose the one you trust most. Write how much water you could add before the tester no longer noticed it.
flow.say: Which method would you trust? How little water can your tester notice?
flow.kid: Choose your best method. Write how little water it can notice.
flow.think: If you improve the tester, does the milk change, or only how sure you are?
flow.parent: A better tester finds smaller amounts, but no tester finds everything.

general: Lean the plate on the same books every time so that the slope is always the same.
Put a tape line across the top and start every drop on it.
Use the same spoon tip, and wash and dry the plate before each try.
creative: Film from the side and count the drops' time over 10 centimetres.
Tape paper lanes so that every drop has its own track.
Add a steel ruler as a groove, so that a drop runs along a straight channel.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own tester and test it on milk with a little water, with half water and with plain water. How little water can your tester notice? Do you think any home tester can find everything?

challenges.title: A seal that shows the jar was opened
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge about trust. A sack or jar can be opened and closed again unseen. You design a seal that shows if it was opened.
challenges.problem: Design a seal for a jar of spice, so that anyone can see if the jar was opened. Then test whether a friend can open and close it without being caught.
constraints: Use paper, tape, thread, a pen and a rubber band.
The seal must be cheap and must hold on a plastic or steel jar.
A friend must try to open the jar and close it again without leaving a sign.
The friend must not be told how your seal works.
The jar must be easy for the owner to open once.
materials: a small plastic or steel jar with a lid
paper strips, tape and a pen
a friend to try to beat the seal

setup.art: A small jar with a paper strip across the lid and down both sides, signed across the join.
setup.caption: 1. Stick a paper strip across the lid and sign across the join.

setup.art: A friend peeling at the paper seal while the child watches.
setup.caption: 2. Ask a friend to try to open the jar without being noticed.

setup.art: A jar with a thread through two holes in the lid and tape, with a torn corner showing.
setup.caption: 3. Try a second design and test it again.

flow.do: Seal the jar with the usual fix. Stick a paper strip across the lid and down both sides, then sign across the join in pen. Ask a friend to try to open and close the jar without leaving a sign. Look to see if you can tell.
flow.say: Can you tell if the jar was opened? How could a friend beat this seal?
flow.kid: Stick a strip across the lid. Sign it. Ask a friend to try to open it secretly.

ask.q: What can a cheat do to beat a simple tape seal?
good: Peel it slowly and stick it back.
Copy the signature.

flow.parent: Do not tell the friend your plan. Let the friend try freely, and be fair to the friend.

flow.do: Make a second seal that is harder to beat. Cut slits in the paper so that it tears when peeled. Or tape a thread across the lid, with a knot, so that it must be cut. Test it again with the friend.
flow.say: What does your friend do this time? Is your seal harder to beat?
flow.kid: Make a seal that tears when it is peeled. Test it again.
flow.parent: Thin paper tears more easily than tape.

flow.do: Try a surprising idea. Sprinkle a few grains of rice under a folded paper flap, so that the grains spill when the flap opens. Or layer tape, paper and tape. Test it with the friend.
flow.say: Would a seller or a buyer want this seal? Why?
flow.kid: Try a surprising seal. Ask a friend to test it.
flow.parent: A seal cannot show what was added before the jar was sealed. It only shows what happened after.

flow.do: Compare the designs. For each one, write whether the friend beat it and how easy it was for the owner to open. Choose the best, and write what a seal can never tell you.
flow.say: Which design was best? What can a seal never tell you?
flow.kid: Choose your best seal. Write what it can never tell you.
flow.think: A seal shows if a jar was opened after it was sealed. What if the cheating happened before?
flow.parent: A seal protects only from the moment it is applied.

general: A paper strip across the lid with a signature across the join.
A tape seal that tears when peeled.
A thread tied through the lid so that it must be cut.
creative: Rice grains under a flap that spill when it is opened.
A layered seal of tape and paper that leaves a mark if it is lifted.
A seal with a number that is written in a notebook, so that a changed number shows.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own seal and test it on a friend. What would make your seal very hard to beat but easy for the owner to open? What can a seal never tell you about the food inside?

worksheets.title: Adding, removing, swapping and the first tests (core)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks that you can tell what adulteration is, why it pays, and which simple test uses which difference.

items.p: Match each trick to its kind of adulteration.
pairs: cream skimmed off milk sold as full-cream
cheap long-grain rice sold as basmati
water poured into a milk can
items.a: as given
items.why: Adding puts in a cheaper thing, removing takes out a valuable part and swapping sells one food as another. In every case the change is secret.

items.p: Sort each one into adulteration or not adulteration.
items: iodine in salt, allowed and named on the packet
brick dust secretly mixed into chilli powder
toned milk sold under the name toned milk
vitamins A and D in fortified oil, named on the label
items.a: as given
items.why: What matters is whether the addition is secret, unallowed or harmful. Open, allowed and labelled additions are not adulteration.

items.p: Water (10 litres) is added to 40 litres of milk at 50 rupees a litre. How many extra rupees?
items.why: Sold as milk, 50 litres at 50 rupees brings 2,500 rupees, and 40 litres brings 2,000. The difference is 500 rupees for water that cost almost nothing.

items.p: A buyer can usually find adulteration in a sealed packet by looking and smelling.
items.why: Adulterants are chosen so that they look and smell like the food, so the buyer's eyes and nose cannot find them.

items.p: Why is saffron cheated far more often than potatoes?
opts: Little weight, big price, so cheating pays
Saffron is easier to grow
Potatoes are never sold by weight
items.why: Cheating pays most where a food costs a lot for its weight. Potatoes are sold by weight too, but they cost little, so the gain is small.

items.p: Which adulterant harms mainly by what it is, and not only by cheating?
opts: Clean water in milk
Used tea leaves in fresh tea
Lead chromate in turmeric
items.why: Lead chromate is a poison that builds up in the body. Clean water and used leaves cheat the buyer of food but are not poisons themselves.

items.p: Lead is stored in the body's ____ because the body mistakes it for calcium.
items.why: The body uses calcium to build bones and takes up lead by mistake, and it stays there for years.

items.p: Put the steps of a fair slanting-plate test in order.
a: Tilt it on the same books
Put a drop of each milk on the same line together
Compare how far each drop ran in 10 seconds
items.why: A clean plate and the same slope keep the test fair. Starting drops together on one line means that only the milk differs.

items.p: A magnet can find brick powder in chilli powder.
items.why: A magnet attracts iron only, and brick powder is not iron. A magnet test suits iron filings in tea.

items.p: Chalk is stirred into sugar. Which difference does the water test use?
opts: Sugar floats and chalk sinks
Sugar dissolves and chalk does not
Sugar is white and chalk is grey
items.why: Sugar vanishes into water, and chalk stays as a cloud and then a layer. Colour is not the difference, since both are white.

items.p: Draw the slanting-plate test. Show the plate, the books, the line and three drops of milk.
items.a: A plate tilted on books, a line across its top, and three drops starting together. Their trails are short, medium and long.
items.why: A fair test needs the same plate, the same slope and a common start line, so that only the milk differs.

items.p: A sample passed every test. Write one honest sentence for the family notebook.
items.a: A good answer says 'nothing found by these tests' and does not say 'pure'. It may add what the tests could not find.
items.why: A test can say 'I found this' but never 'there is nothing here', so the honest words are 'nothing found'.

items.p: Is milk pure?

views.says: Pure means one substance only. Milk is a mixture of water, fat, protein and milk sugar, so it is never pure.
Milk is pure if it meets the written standard and nothing was added or taken away.
Pure means natural, as it came from the cow.

items.ask: Which meaning would you use when you buy milk, and why?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer sees that each meaning is useful for something. The chemist's meaning fits no food, the legal one lets inspectors act and the shopper's one can include natural poisons.
items.why: The three meanings answer different questions, and the word pure alone does not tell you which one is meant.

items.p: A pink dye made for cloth is found in cotton candy. Why is it adulteration and not a permitted addition?
opts: Pink is not a food colour
Cotton candy is not a real food
Not allowed in food, and hidden
items.why: Eight artificial colours are allowed in certain foods, in set amounts, and named on the label. A cloth dye is not one of them.

items.p: Name two things on a packet that a family can check before buying, and say what each tells.
items.a: The 14-digit licence number shows that the business is registered. The batch number lets a bad lot be traced. The date, the address and the ingredients also count.
items.why: A label cannot show a secret addition, but it makes tracing and reporting possible.

items.p: A family finds that a test shows something odd in a packet of turmeric. What should they do first?
opts: Throw the packet away quietly
Taste a little to check
Tell nobody
Repeat it, keep the packet, ask for help
items.why: One try can be a fluke, so repeat it. Keeping the packet and the bill lets the food authority test it, and tasting an unknown sample is never safe.

worksheets.title: What a test can and cannot tell (stretch)
worksheets.context: This sheet goes further. It asks what a passing test means, how cheats aim at tests, and what packets and laws add.

items.p: A honey sample passes the test of a drop that holds together in water. What does this show?
opts: That the honey is made from nectar
Only that it is thick
That no sugar was added
items.why: The test checks thickness, and bees make honey by drying nectar until it is thick. A syrup can be as thick, so it passes too.

items.p: A test that finds nothing proves that a food is pure.
items.why: A test can find only what it was built for, and only above its smallest amount. 'Nothing found' is all it can say.

items.p: Before anyone adds anything, about ____ parts in every 100 parts of milk are water.
items.why: Milk is a mixture, and most of it is water. Adding water changes the mix, not the kind of substance.

items.p: On wet paper, one colour travels farther than another. What does this show?
opts: It clings less, so water carries it farther
It is the better dye
It is heavier
items.why: Each dye clings to paper by a different amount, so the water carries them different distances. That separates the dyes.

items.p: Which test would catch each adulterant?
items.a: as given
items.why: Each test uses one difference: dissolving or sinking, attraction to iron, how fast a drop runs, and colour with starch.

items.p: Match each adulterant to the difference that its test uses.
items.a: as given
items.why: A test works by finding one difference between the food and the thing that was added.

items.p: Put these in order, from the drop that runs slowest on a slanting plate to the one that runs fastest.
items.why: More water makes the liquid thinner, so the drop runs faster. The quarter-water milk is close to plain milk, so the first two are hard to tell apart.

items.p: A dairy checks milk with a lactometer. Say how cheats fooled it, and why.
items.a: The lactometer notices thin milk. Cheats added sugar, starch or salt to bring the thickness back. The test measured one property that stands for quality, and the cheats supplied only that property.
items.why: When a test checks one property, cheats can restore that property alone.

items.p: A seller adds clean water to milk. Why does the law still treat it as an offence?
opts: Clean water is a poison
Milk must never be mixed with anything
The family pays for more than it gets
items.why: Harm by cheating is real, even when nothing poisonous is added. The family loses money and nourishment.

items.p: Iodine in salt is welcome and chalk in sugar is a crime. Say what three things separate them.
items.a: The iodine has been tested and is allowed, it is within a limit and the label says so. The chalk is hidden, unallowed and a cheat.
items.why: An addition is not adulteration if it is allowed, within the limit and declared.

items.p: Is food in sealed packets safer than loose food?

views.says: A packet has a licence number and a batch number, so a bad lot can be traced to a maker.

views.who: A buyer of loose whole spice
views.says: Loose whole food can be seen, smelled and tested, and the seller has a face you know.

views.who: A family on a small budget
views.says: Packets cost more, and a cheaper loose food may be all we can buy.

items.ask: Which view would you give a friend, and what would you want to know first?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer notes that the 2020 honey tests found failures in big brands, and that tracing needs a packet. Neither view is always right.
items.why: Evidence supports packets for some foods, such as oils, and not for all. Cost also decides what a family can do.

items.p: Toned milk sold under that name is adulterated milk.
items.why: It has had fat taken out openly, and it says so on the packet, so nobody is cheated about what it is.

items.p: Turmeric has lead at 30 parts per million. The limit is 10. How many times the limit?
items.why: 30 ÷ 10 = 3. The sample holds three times the limit.

items.p: Draw a paper strip after 10 minutes in water, with a green dot split into two colours.
items.a: A strip standing in water with a pencil line near the bottom. A yellow band travelled farther and a blue band stayed lower. A mark shows where the water reached.
items.why: Different dyes cling by different amounts, so they separate into bands at different heights.

items.p: A label says 'no added colour', but a laboratory finds a dye. Which kind of bad food is this?
opts: Sub-standard, because it is cheap
Misbranded, because the label says something untrue
Unsafe, because it has a label
items.why: A false label makes the food misbranded. A dye may also make it unsafe, but the label is the first fault.

items.p: A family's test shows something. Write what they should keep and what they should do next.
items.a: Keep the packet, the bill and the batch number. Repeat the test once. Report it to the food authority through the Food Safety Connect app or the state food safety office.
items.why: Evidence kept is what the food authority needs to trace and test the lot.

worksheets.title: Faulty claims and open questions (challenge)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks you to spot faulty reasoning about tests and surveys and to weigh debates that scientists have not settled.

items.p: A girl says, 'My turmeric left the water pale, so it has no lead.' What is wrong with her claim?
opts: The water was too cold
Turmeric never holds lead
The test misses lead, which does not dissolve
items.why: A test can find only what it uses a difference for. Lead chromate hardly dissolves, so a water test cannot show it.

items.p: A school tests 10 samples and finds nothing. Which claim can the school fairly make?
opts: All the food in the town is pure
These tests found nothing in these 10 samples
Nobody cheats in this town
items.why: Ten samples are a small part of a town's food, and the tests have limits. The honest claim is only about what was tested.

items.p: A new test can raise the cases reported, though the food did not change.
items.why: A new test finds what the old tests could not see. So counts show what is looked for as well as what exists.

items.p: Milk has 87 parts water in every 100. A half-milk, half-water mix has ____ parts water in every 100.
items.why: Half water and half milk gives (100 + 87) ÷ 2 = 93.5 per hundred parts of water. The jump from 87 is only 6.5, so a test can easily miss it.

items.p: Many Delhi families fell ill together in 1998. What does that say about loose oil from one source?
items.a: One source of oil reached many families, so one poisoned batch harmed many. It is hard to trace loose oil, and it shows why batch numbers and sealed packets help.
items.why: A long chain with loose food makes one fault spread, and a lack of tracing makes it hard to stop.

items.p: Order from easiest to hardest to find with a glass of water and a spoon.
items.why: Chalk settles in water and a dye runs. A small amount of added water barely changes a drop. Lead chromate cannot be found without a laboratory.

items.p: Kesari dal is banned in most of India. Should it stay banned?

views.who: A doctor who has seen lathyrism
views.says: People eating mostly kesari dal for months have lost the use of their legs. A ban protects them.

views.who: A farmer in a dry district
views.says: The grass pea grows when other crops fail. A ban takes away a drought food and a crop that fixes nitrogen.
Varieties with little of the harmful substance exist, so a rule could allow only these.

items.ask: What would you want to know before you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer asks who eats it, how much and for how long, and whether the low-toxin varieties are used. No view is marked right, because scientists still disagree.
items.why: The harm comes from eating mostly one pulse for months, so the question is not simply safe or unsafe.

items.p: A rat tastes a little new food and waits. You test turmeric in water. Is that the same thing?
items.a: Both test before trusting, in small amounts, and both can miss what the test cannot show. The rat tests with her body and a delay, and you use a chosen difference.
items.why: Testing a little before trusting a lot is a way living beings protect themselves, and every test has limits.

items.p: Which is the worst way to say how common adulteration is?
opts: Giving one percentage without saying what was counted
Saying how many samples were tested
Saying what the standard was
items.why: A survey may count failing a quality standard, finding an accidental contaminant or finding a harmful adulterant. These give very different numbers.

items.p: Sort each one into a stand-in measurement or a direct check.
items: a magnet pulling iron out of tea
a drop that holds together read as honey
reading the DNA of a rice grain
bright yellow read as good turmeric
items.a: as given
items.why: A stand-in measures an easy thing that usually goes with quality. A cheat can supply the easy thing without the quality.

items.p: Match each situation to the reason a test failed.
pairs: the test measured nitrogen, which melamine has
sugar was added to bring back the thickness
lead was missed by a water test
items.a: as given
items.why: Each test measured one property, and the cheat or the chemistry supplied that property.

items.p: Draw the chain from a turmeric field to your kitchen. Mark where you can look and where you cannot.
items.a: A row of boxes: field, trader, mill, packer, shop, kitchen. A tick where someone can see the food. A cross where the food is hidden, such as inside a sealed sack or packet.
items.why: Cheating can enter wherever the food is hidden from the next person.

items.p: India's limit for lead in turmeric is 10 milligrams in every kilogram. How many milligrams are allowed in a 500 gram packet?
items.why: 500 grams is half a kilogram, so half of 10 is 5 milligrams.

items.p: Calcium carbide gives a gas like ethylene, so it is a safe way to ripen mangoes.
items.why: The gas it gives off is similar to ethylene, but the stones carry poisonous impurities. The use is banned in India. Ethylene itself is permitted.

items.p: 'Natural' and 'safe' mean the same thing. Give one example from this lesson that shows they do not.
items.a: Argemone seeds are completely natural but poison mustard oil. Kesari dal is natural and can cause lathyrism when eaten alone for months.
items.why: Nature makes poisons as well as foods, so a word like natural cannot stand in for a test or a standard.

opts: A permitted colour named on a sweet packet
Brick dust secretly mixed into chilli powder
Toned milk sold as toned milk
quiz.why: Adulteration is secret. Open, allowed and labelled additions are not. A child who picks another answer may think any addition counts.

quiz.p: A seller secretly skims the fat from milk and still calls it full-cream. What kind of adulteration is this?
opts: Adding a cheaper thing
Swapping one food for another
Removing a valuable part
quiz.why: The seller takes out the valuable fat and keeps the name. Adding and swapping would need something new to be put in.

quiz.p: One turmeric seller adds dye for brightness, and buyers cannot tell. What happens to the honest seller?
opts: Loses customers to the bright turmeric
Gets more customers
Nothing changes
quiz.why: If buyers cannot tell good from bad, they may not pay more for the honest one, and the cheat can win. Akerlof wrote about this in 1970.

quiz.p: Which food is most likely to be adulterated?
opts: Potatoes, because they are everywhere
Plain water, because it is free
Saffron, because a small weight costs a lot
quiz.why: A cheat gains most where a food costs a lot for its weight. Potatoes are cheap, so the gain is small.

quiz.p: Which adulterant harms mainly by cheating and not by poisoning?
opts: Lead chromate in turmeric
Clean water in milk
Argemone oil in mustard oil
quiz.why: Clean water is not a poison, but the family pays for milk and gets less nourishment. The other two harm by what they are.

quiz.p: Why does lead harm a young child more than a grown-up?
opts: A child eats far more turmeric
Lead is harmless to adults
Children absorb more lead, and their brains grow
quiz.why: Children absorb about four to five times as much of the lead they swallow, and their brains are still being built.

quiz.p: A teaspoon of turmeric on still water gives bright yellow streaks at once. What does this suggest?
opts: Lead chromate is present
The turmeric is strong and pure
A dye that dissolves may be present
quiz.why: Natural turmeric hardly dissolves, so a quick bright colour points to a dye. The test cannot show lead chromate, which does not dissolve.

quiz.p: Iron filings were mixed into tea. Which test could catch it?
opts: A magnet, because only iron is attracted
The glass of water, because iron dissolves
The iodine drop, because iron turns blue-black
quiz.why: A test uses one difference. Iron is attracted to a magnet, and it does not dissolve and does not react with iodine like starch.

quiz.p: You test two milks on a slanting plate. Which makes the test fair?
opts: Tilt the plate more for the watered milk
Same plate, slope and drop size, started together
A bigger drop of the plain-looking milk
quiz.why: A fair test changes only the milk. Changing the slope or the drop size would change two things at once.

quiz.p: A turmeric sample leaves the water pale. What can you say?
opts: It has no lead chromate
Nothing found. This test cannot see lead
It is pure
quiz.why: Each test finds one kind of thing, above a smallest amount. A water test cannot show lead chromate, which does not dissolve.

quiz.p: Cheats added melamine to milk, and the protein test said 'plenty of protein'. Why?
opts: It measured nitrogen, which melamine is full of
Melamine is a protein
The test was never used
quiz.why: Nitrogen stands in for protein. Melamine supplied the nitrogen without the protein, so the test was fooled.

quiz.p: A packet says 'pure milk'. A chemist says milk is not pure. How can both be right?
opts: The chemist has not tested the milk
The packet is always lying
One substance only, but milk is a mixture
quiz.why: In chemistry pure means one substance only. In food law it means meeting a standard with nothing hidden. The meanings differ.

opts: A permitted colour hiding stale food in secret
Declared iodine in salt, within the limit
A cloth dye in a sweet
quiz.why: Allowed, within the limit and declared. A permitted colour used secretly breaks the third rule, and a cloth dye is never allowed.

quiz.p: A 14-digit licence number is printed on a packet. What does it tell you?
opts: The business is registered and can be traced
This packet was tested in a laboratory
The food is free of adulterants
quiz.why: It shows that the maker is registered, so a complaint can be traced. It does not show that this packet was tested.

quiz.p: A family finds a worrying result on a spice. What is the best first step?
opts: Mix it with the rest of the stock
Repeat, keep the packet and bill, report it
Throw it away and say nothing
quiz.why: One try can be a fluke, and a kept packet with a bill lets the food authority test the lot. Quietly throwing it away leaves others at risk.

maths.problem: A cup of whole milk is about 87 per cent water. A cup holds 4 spoons, made of 2 spoons of milk and 2 spoons of added water. About what share of the cup is water? Compare it with plain milk.
maths.answer: About 93.5 per cent, compared with 87 per cent. The share rises by only about 6.5 percentage points.
maths.explain: 2 spoons of milk hold 2 × 0.87 = 1.74 spoons of water. Add 2 spoons of added water to get 3.74 spoons of water in 4 spoons. 3.74 ÷ 4 = 0.935, which is 93.5 per cent. Plain milk is 87 per cent, so half-and-half milk is only about 6.5 points higher.
maths.context: This problem uses the milk cups of the mystery test to show how big the change in water really is.
maths.why_maths: Even half added water changes the share of water only a little, because milk is mostly water already. That is why a test has trouble noticing small amounts.

maths.problem: A seller has 100 litres of milk. Imagine a test that notices added water only above 30 parts in every 100 of the mixture. How many litres can the seller add and not be noticed?
maths.answer: Up to about 42 litres is not noticed. About 43 litres or above would be.
maths.explain: Water added is x litres, and the mixture is 100 + x litres. We want x ÷ (100 + x) to be 0.30. So x = 0.30 × (100 + x), which gives 0.7x = 30 and x is about 42.9 litres. Anything under 42 litres stays under the limit of the test.
maths.context: This problem uses an imagined test limit to show how a seller can stay below the smallest amount a test can notice.
maths.why_maths: Every test has a smallest amount it can see. This sum shows how much a cheat can add without crossing it.

maths.problem: India's limit for lead in turmeric is 10 parts per million, which is 10 milligrams in every kilogram. A sample holds 300 times the limit. How many milligrams of lead are in a 100 gram packet?
maths.explain: 300 times 10 is 3,000 milligrams in each kilogram. A 100 gram packet is one tenth of a kilogram, so 3,000 ÷ 10 = 300 milligrams.
maths.context: This problem uses the limit for lead in turmeric to show how a part per million is worked out in a packet.
maths.why_maths: Parts per million is how scientists write very small amounts, and the same ratio works for any packet size.

maths.problem: A survey tested 6,432 milk samples. It found 12 samples of unsafe adulterated milk, and about 41 out of every 100 samples below quality standards. About how many samples were below standard? About how many times more is that than 12?
maths.answer: About 2,637 samples, which is roughly 220 times as many as 12.
maths.explain: 41 ÷ 100 × 6,432 = 2,637 samples. And 2,637 ÷ 12 is roughly 220. The two counts differ because they count different things.
maths.context: This problem uses the figures of a national milk survey. It shows how different counts of the same food give very different numbers.
maths.why_maths: A percentage means nothing until you know what was counted. A ratio of two counts shows how far apart two definitions are.

maths.problem: In the chromatography test, the water travels 60 millimetres up the paper. A yellow band stops 54 millimetres up and a blue band stops 24 millimetres up. Work out each band's distance divided by the water's distance. Which dye clings more to the paper?
maths.answer: Yellow 54 ÷ 60 = 0.9, blue 24 ÷ 60 = 0.4. The blue dye clings more.
maths.explain: A band that moves almost as far as the water, 0.9, clings little to the paper. A band that moves less, 0.4, clings more. The same dye on the same paper gives about the same number each time, so the number helps name a dye.
maths.context: This problem uses the numbers from a paper strip test to compare how far two dyes travelled.
maths.why_maths: A ratio of distances stays the same for a dye on a given paper. So it can help to identify the dye.

spotted.text: At the kitchen counter, hold a packet of turmeric or a bag of rice next to the same food sold loose. Notice that the packet has a printed licence number and a batch number, and the loose food has none. Ask what that tells you about who can trace it.
spotted.art: A packet and an open sack of rice side by side on a kitchen counter with a finger pointing at a printed number.

spotted.text: On a milk packet in the fridge, look for the word toned, double toned or full cream. Notice that the packet names what has been done to the milk, and that this is why it is not adulterated.
spotted.art: A milk pouch with the words toned milk circled and a fat percentage beside them.

spotted.text: At the sweet shop, look at a very bright orange or pink sweet next to a pale one. Notice the colour, and ask what the packet says about colour. A permitted colour must be named.
spotted.art: A tray of sweets with one very bright orange sweet and a shop label with a list of colours.

spotted.text: At the fruit seller's stall in mango season, look at a pile of mangoes. Notice whether the colour is even and whether the skin is spotted. Ask how the seller ripens them. Fruit ripen with a gas they make themselves, and stones that give off a similar gas are banned.
spotted.art: A fruit seller with a pile of mangoes in different colours, and a child looking closely at one.

spotted.text: At the grocery, pick up a bottle of mustard oil or ghee and look at its seal and its label. Notice if the seal is whole, and if the batch number and date are printed.
spotted.art: A hand lifting a sealed oil bottle with a thumb on the seal and a printed batch number.

spotted.text: In the tea cup, drop a pinch of tea leaves into plain water. Watch how fast the colour comes out. Notice that natural tea colours water slowly, and that this is one reason added colour can be found.
spotted.art: A clear glass of water with a pinch of tea leaves and a faint brown trail beginning.

spotted.text: At the corner shop, look at the salt packet. Notice the word iodised and the blue plus F mark. Ask why a nutrient that is added openly is not adulteration.
spotted.art: A salt packet with the word iodised and a small blue plus F sign.

spotted.text: At the weekly market, notice how many hands a sack of turmeric or rice passes through between the field and your bag. Ask which of them you could ask a question.
spotted.art: A weekly market with sacks of spices, a seller, a buyer and a child looking at a sack.

applications: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India sends mobile testing vans, called Food Safety on Wheels, to markets in many states. Families can bring a sample to be tested for common adulterants. Ask your local food safety office where the van visits.
Dairies measure milk at the gate with a lactometer, and many test for fat and added water. If a farmer's milk is found watered, it can be refused or priced lower, which pays an honest farmer better.

After researchers in Bangladesh linked lead in village blood to turmeric, the government warned traders, checked markets and fined sellers. Lead in market turmeric later fell. Testing and law together can work.

Erode in Tamil Nadu is one of India's big turmeric centres. A trader there can send a sample of a lot to a laboratory before it is ground. Then a problem is found before it reaches a thousand kitchens.
Honey from a beekeeper you know, bought near the hive, has a short chain. A short chain means you can ask the beekeeper how it was made, which a long chain does not allow.
A school canteen can buy whole spices and grind them in the school kitchen. Then nobody can add anything. It costs more time, and it can feed many children safely.
The Food Safety Connect app and the helpline 1915 let any family report a suspected case. A kept packet and bill help the food officer trace the lot back through the chain.
Scientists at the Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics in Hyderabad developed a DNA test for basmati rice. It helps show that a sack is truly basmati. Then honest farmers are paid fairly.
ask_kids: Which food at home do you think could be cheated, and why would a cheat choose it?
If a test finds nothing, what exactly can you say? What can you not say?
Milk is mostly water. So why is adding more water wrong?
Why do you think buyers pick the brightest turmeric, and what might that make a seller do?
Salt has iodine added on purpose, and chalk in sugar is a crime. What is the difference?
A rat tastes a tiny bit of a new food and waits. When do you test a food before you trust it?
Who could you ask in your own market to learn where the food comes from?
What would you want to know about a test before you trusted its answer?

jokes.j: What did the sugar say to the chalk in the glass of water?
jokes.a: 'I am off to dissolve into the conversation. You can stay at the bottom and think about it.'

jokes.j: Why did the magnet get the job at the tea stall?
jokes.a: It was very attractive, and it always picked out what did not belong.

jokes.j: What did the milk say when it was shaken in a bottle with a drop of detergent?
jokes.a: 'I only came for a quiet foam. Now I am a bubble bath.'

jokes.j: What did the iodine say when it met a potato?
jokes.a: 'Wow, you are full of starch!' Then it went blue-black with excitement, and nobody could calm it down.

jokes.j: Why did the turmeric refuse to take the water test?
jokes.a: It was afraid of showing its true colours. Then it stayed pale and passed, and it still could not say it was pure.

jokes.j: Why was the lactometer the gloomiest tool at the dairy?
jokes.a: Every time the milk got thinner, it sank.

jokes.j: What does a paper napkin say to a dye that has run away?
jokes.a: 'I know where you have been. You left a stain.'

jokes.j: Why did the chalk stay at the bottom of the glass?
jokes.a: It never learned to mix. It just settled down in a corner.

jokes.j: What did the tester say when the turmeric passed every test?
jokes.a: 'Nothing found. That is all I am allowed to say. I am a tester, not a fortune teller.'

buy.item: Food colouring in yellow, red or green (liquid or powder)
buy.why: Used by the grown-up to secretly colour tea and turmeric for the mystery cups, and for the paper strip test. About ₹30 to ₹80 for a small pack of three.
buy.plan: Any bright food colour from a baker's shop works. Do not use a brown one for tea. A bright red sweet-coating or a few drops of red kumkum water also work.

buy.item: Tincture of iodine, a small bottle (optional)
buy.why: For the starch activity, used only by a grown-up. About ₹20 to ₹60 from a medical shop. It stains and must never be swallowed.
buy.plan: If you do not have it, skip the starch activity. The game and the lesson work without it.

buy.why: Crushed to a fine powder for the 'chalk in sugar' cup. About ₹10 for a box from a stationery shop.
buy.plan: A pinch of dry eggshell ground very fine in a mortar also makes a white cloud in water.

buy.item: Coffee filter paper or white kitchen paper towel
buy.why: For the paper strips in the colour test. About ₹50 to ₹150 for coffee filters.
buy.plan: A white paper napkin or kitchen tissue works. Newspaper does not, because its ink runs.

buy.item: Washable felt pens, black and brown
buy.why: For the colour-splitting test. About ₹30 to ₹100. Check that the label says washable or water-based.
buy.plan: Use the colours of any washable pen. A green food colouring dot is enough on its own.

buy.item: A hand lens or magnifying glass
buy.why: To look closely at grains, seeds and powders. About ₹50 to ₹150.
buy.plan: A phone camera zoomed in works well.

buy.item: A small magnet with iron filings (optional)
buy.why: For the optional magnet step. A magnet is about ₹20 to ₹60 and filings about ₹30 from a hardware shop or a school science kit.
buy.plan: Skip the magnet step if you cannot find filings. The game card teaches the same idea.

buy.item: Small clear plastic bottles with lids
buy.why: For the shake test. Any 200 millilitre bottle with a screw lid, about ₹10 to ₹20 each.
buy.plan: A clean water bottle or a plastic jar with a lid works.

buy.why: For draining curd. About ₹30 to ₹80 for a metre.
buy.plan: A clean thin cotton handkerchief or an old dupatta that has been washed well works.

buy.item: Printing for the game and the worksheets
buy.why: Printing about 6 pages of game cards and 3 pages of worksheets. About ₹2 to ₹10 a page at a print shop.
buy.plan: Copy the case cards by hand on index cards or scrap paper, and write the eight test names on slips.

buy.item: A book about food and the people who grow it
buy.why: A parent can read from a book about food or farming aloud before the story. Library or second-hand copies cost much less than new.
buy.plan: Ask at the school or town library, or borrow from a friend.
